The provided abstract describes a comprehensive review paper on nanofluid minimum quantity lubrication (NMQL) in machining, covering preparation, fluid/thermal/tribological properties, supply equipment, atomization mechanisms, and performance across turning, milling, and grinding. The specific quantitative examples cited in the abstract involve jatropha oil-based alumina nanofluids (85% reduction in coefficient of friction compared with dry conditions), alumina nanoparticle cutting fluids (177-230% tool life improvement in hard milling), and carbon nanotube nanoparticles in normal saline (145.06% increase in convective heat transfer coefficient).

Hypothesis 1 proposes titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanoparticles (20-40 nm, 0.5-1.0 vol%) in vegetable oil creating an adaptive thermal conductivity shift (0.15 to 0.45 W/mK between 35°C and 85°C). None of these materials, concentrations, temperature ranges, or thermal conductivity values appear in the abstract.

Hypothesis 2 proposes electrostatic atomization with 2% (w/v) silicon dioxide nanoparticles and 10% (v/v) magnetorheological fluid in MQL, targeting at least 40% tool wear reduction and 30% Ra improvement under specific cutting parameters. None of these formulations, atomization methods, test conditions, or quantitative outcomes are supported by the abstract.

Hypothesis 3 proposes electrostatic atomization with silicon dioxide nanoparticles in a biolubricant for turning at 100 m/min, targeting at least 30% friction coefficient reduction and 25% wear rate reduction. The abstract does not mention electrostatic atomization, silicon dioxide nanoparticles, or these specific turning parameters and reduction thresholds.

Hypothesis 4 proposes a dynamically controlled MQL system using surface-modified copper oxide (CuO) nanoparticles in bio-based ester oil with concentration modulated by real-time temperature and vibration data on AISI 1045 steel and AlSi10Mg alloy. None of these materials, control mechanisms, workpieces, or quantitative targets are present in the abstract.
